recipe.history: Blue cheese — and specifically the great blue-veined cheeses of France, England, and Italy, Roquefort, Stilton, and Gorgonzola — is among the most ancient and storied of all fermented dairy products, with origin stories that blur the line between history and legend. Roquefort is often cited as the oldest documented cheese in the world: a 1411 charter granted by Charles VI of France gave the people of Roquefort-sur-Soulzon the exclusive right to age their cheese in the natural limestone caves of the Combalou plateau, where the naturally occurring Penicillium roqueforti mold colonizes the paste and produces the distinctive blue-green veining, the sharp, pungent, complex flavor, and the creamy, crumbling texture that makes Roquefort one of the genuinely irreplaceable ingredients in European cooking. Gorgonzola, the Italian blue cheese made in Piedmont and Lombardy since at least the ninth century CE, takes its name from the small town east of Milan where, according to legend, a cheesemaker left his curd out overnight and returned in the morning to find it had been transformed by mold into something extraordinary. Stilton, England's great contribution to the blue cheese canon, was first recorded in the early eighteenth century, sold to travelers at an inn on the Great North Road. All three belong to the same family of radical transformation: fresh milk, acted upon by specific molds and cultures and time, becoming something that bears almost no relationship to its origin — complex, pungent, savory, and capable of elevating almost any dish it encounters. Collard greens are equally storied, with origins in the eastern Mediterranean and a history in American cooking that is inseparable from the history of African American foodways in the South.
recipe.history2: Collard greens — Brassica oleracea var. viridis — are among the oldest cultivated brassicas, grown for food in Greece and Rome and carried into the Americas by European colonizers in the seventeenth century. In the American South, collard greens became the cornerstone of African American cooking not by choice but by necessity: enslaved people on Southern plantations were often given the parts of the pig and the produce of the kitchen garden that their enslavers did not want, and collards — tough, bitter, requiring long cooking — became through skill and patience a dish of extraordinary richness and depth. Long-braised with smoked ham hocks, pork fatback, or neck bones, collards are transformed over hours of slow cooking from fibrous and harsh to silky, yielding, and deeply savory, their bitterness converted by heat into something sweetly vegetal that carries the smoke and pork flavor of the braising liquid into every bite. This technique — using the alchemy of time, heat, and smoke to transform something tough into something extraordinary — is a defining contribution of African American cooking to American cuisine, and collard greens are its most celebrated expression. The combination of bleu cheese and collard greens on a burger is an audacious pairing: the pungent, rich funk of the blue cheese meeting the smoky, slightly bitter, deeply savory greens, both layered over the fat and char of a beef patty, creates a combination that is simultaneously Southern and cosmopolitan, humble and sophisticated.
recipe.history3_personal: I ate my first properly made pot of collard greens at a small barbecue restaurant in North Carolina, at a table covered with butcher paper, in the company of people who grew up eating this food and therefore ordered the greens without thinking and ate them without commentary, as the obvious and necessary accompaniment to everything else. I ordered them because everyone else did, without quite knowing what I was agreeing to. They arrived in a small bowl, deep olive-drab green, glistening with pot liquor that was more savory than any broth I had ever tasted, scented with smoke and pork and something faintly sweet that I could not immediately identify. The greens themselves were silky and gave way immediately, the bitterness I had feared entirely absent, replaced by a flavor so rich and layered that I ate the whole bowl and then quietly asked for another. I asked the woman who brought it what made the pot liquor taste the way it did. She said ham hock and patience. I have been making collards with ham hock and patience ever since. The first time I put them on a burger with a crumble of Gorgonzola it made sense the way a very good idea always makes sense — obviously, inevitably, and slightly embarrassingly late.
recipe.history4_philosophy: The Bleu Collard Burger is a burger of big, unapologetic flavors, and it demands a patty cooked to medium rare — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit — not as a technicality but as a philosophical statement. The bleu cheese brings funk and fat and a sharp, lingering pungency. The collard greens bring smoke and deep vegetable savoriness and a yielding, silky texture. The patty must bring juice and richness and the mineral depth of well-handled beef. At medium rare, all three elements are in balance: the patty's juiciness dilutes nothing but provides the foundation upon which the blue cheese and collards can perform. The fat of the patty carries the flavor of the blue cheese across the palate; the patty's slight char mirrors the smokiness of the braised greens. Cook the patty past medium rare and you reduce it to a structural element rather than a flavor contributor — dry and gray, capable of holding the toppings but not of speaking alongside them. A well-done patty in this burger is the culinary equivalent of inviting two great musicians to perform and then turning off the main microphone. The blue cheese and collards are worth more than that. So is the beef.
ingredients: 1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp water (egg wash)
1 large bunch fresh collard greens (about 500g), stems removed, leaves roughly chopped
1 smoked ham hock (about 400g) or 150g thick-cut smoked bacon, diced
170g quality blue cheese (Gorgonzola dolce, Maytag Blue, or Roquefort), softened
4 thick slices sharp white cheddar or additional blue cheese for melting
instructions: 1. Braise the collard greens (can be made up to 3 days ahead, improves with time): If using a ham hock, place it in a large pot with chicken stock and 240ml of water over medium heat. Bring to a simmer and cook 30 minutes to begin rendering fat and flavor into the liquid. If using bacon, render it in the pot over medium heat until the fat has rendered out, about 8 minutes; remove and set aside.

2. Add diced onion to the pot and cook in the fat until softened, about 6 minutes. Add garlic and cook 2 more minutes. Add the chopped collard greens in batches, stirring to wilt between additions. Once all greens are in the pot, add stock (and ham hock if using), apple cider vinegar, red pepper flakes, salt, sugar, and black pepper. Bring to a simmer, reduce heat to low, cover, and cook for 45–60 minutes until the greens are completely tender and silky. Taste and adjust salt and vinegar. Stir in butter to enrich. Keep warm or refrigerate and reheat.

3. Make the honey-bacon glaze: Cook bacon strips in a skillet over medium heat until most of the fat has rendered but the bacon is not yet crisp, about 5 minutes. In a small bowl, combine honey, apple cider vinegar, and cayenne. Pour the honey mixture over the bacon in the pan. Increase heat to medium-high and continue cooking, turning the bacon frequently, until the glaze has caramelized and the bacon is lacquered and sticky, 3–5 more minutes. Transfer to parchment to cool slightly. It will be very sticky.

4. Make the bleu cheese spread: Mash softened blue cheese with a fork until fairly smooth but with some texture remaining. Fold in crème fraîche, lemon juice, and black pepper until combined. Taste — adjust with more lemon or pepper as needed. Refrigerate until needed but remove from refrigerator 20 minutes before assembling.

5. Make the buns: Combine flour, yeast, sugar, and salt in a stand mixer with the dough hook. Add warm milk, water, and egg. Mix on low 2 minutes, then medium 4 minutes. Add softened butter one tablespoon at a time. Mix on medium-high 6–8 minutes until smooth and elastic. Rise covered in an oiled bowl 1–1.5 hours until doubled.

6. Divide bun dough into 4 portions, shape into tight balls, place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, flatten gently. Proof covered 45–60 minutes. Brush with egg wash. Bake at 375°F / 190°C for 15–18 minutes until deep golden. Cool completely.

7. Form the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 equal portions (about 225g each). Press into round patties 3/4 inch thick and 4 inches wide. Press a dimple in the center. Season both sides with salt, black pepper, and smoked paprika just before cooking.

8. Cook the patties: Heat a cast iron skillet over high heat for 3 minutes until smoking. Add a thin film of neutral oil. Place patties in the skillet. Cook undisturbed 3 minutes to build a deeply caramelized crust.

9. Flip once. Place a thick slice of white cheddar (or a large crumble of blue cheese) on each patty. Cook 2–3 more minutes, covering the pan in the last minute to melt the cheese. Check internal temperature — target 130–135°F / 54–57°C for medium rare. Remove from heat and rest 3–4 minutes on a wire rack.

10. Warm the collard greens: If made ahead, rewarm gently over medium-low heat until hot and fragrant. Using tongs or a slotted spoon, lift the greens from their liquid, draining well. The greens should be tender and yielding, not waterlogged.
11. Toast the buns: Slice buns and toast cut-side down in a lightly buttered skillet over medium heat until golden, 1–2 minutes.

12. Assemble: Spread a generous layer of bleu cheese spread on both cut sides of the bun. Place the rested, cheese-topped patty on the bottom bun. Add a tangle of drained braised collard greens directly over the patty — be generous. Lay a strip of honey-glazed bacon over the greens. Add a few slices of red onion. Crumble additional fresh blue cheese over everything. Close with the top bun and serve immediately, with extra collard pot liquor available for dipping if desired.
